title: Nigeria Anopheles Vector Database: An Overview of 100 Years' Research
relevance_reason: The paper uses 'vector' in the entomological sense (disease-transmitting mosquitoes) and 'database' as a compilation of published entomological records; it has no connection to vector database technology, vector indexing, or similarity/nearest-neighbor search.
research_focus: A comprehensive collation of 100 years of published data (1900–2010) on the spatial distribution, species composition, sampling methods, insecticide resistance, and parasite prevalence of Anopheles mosquito vectors of malaria and lymphatic filariasis in Nigeria.
method: All 110 relevant publications were collated into a georeferenced database recording locality, latitude/longitude, time period, species, abundance, sampling/collection methods, morphological and molecular identification methods, insecticide resistance status (including kdr allele), and parasite prevalence rates.
results_summary: The collation of 110 publications identified 484,747 Anopheles mosquitoes across 632 spatially unique descriptions at 142 georeferenced locations in Nigeria. The most abundant vectors were the An. gambiae complex (65.2%) and An. funestus complex (17.3%), with molecular forms M and S identified at 120 locations. Insecticide resistance to pyrethroids and organochlorines was widespread across 45 locations, particularly in the southwestern region. The data revealed a geographical shift in research focus from the northern region in the 20th century to the southern region in recent decades, with large gaps in the eastern regions. The database provides a baseline for malaria and LF vector control programmes in Nigeria.
limitations: Total number of mosquitoes collected is underrepresented as numbers were not available in some studies; Species abundance was not specified in some studies; Very few studies were carried out in the same locations in different years or seasons, restricting analysis and comparisons over time; Great variability in reporting of mosquito sampling and collection methods over time; Most missing data were from earlier studies (1900–1963) when few identification options existed; Few records on LF parasite prevalence make it difficult for comparisons between studies, locations, and species
research_gaps: Research on the composition and distribution of the An. funestus group is needed as it is an important vector for both LF and malaria; The role of An. gambiae M and S molecular forms in malaria and/or LF transmission and how they interact is largely unknown; Large gaps in data from the eastern regions of Nigeria; Very little research done in the northwestern region, especially the Garki Project area; Need for widespread systematic sampling across the country; Need for standardized methods for sampling, collection, and species identification; Need for better linkages and partnerships between entomologists, parasitologists, national control programmes, and international donors
